items.title: You can buy crystals of a 'noble gas' compound by the gram
items.claim: Xenon difluoride (XeF2) is sold by chemical suppliers. Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4) was first synthesised in 1962 by Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne National Lab. The textbook claim that noble gases 'do not react' was overturned 60 years ago.
items.prompt: What made xenon chemistry possible in 1962?

options.text: Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed xenon's first ionisation energy (1170 kJ/mol) is almost identical to O2's (1175 kJ/mol). Since PtF6 oxidised O2, he tried Xe + PtF6 — and got XePtF6, the first noble gas compound
Lasers were finally powerful enough to break Xe bonds

items.reveal:
In early 1962 Bartlett had been making PtF6 — a brilliant red solid — and noticed a sample turned red on contact with air. Analysis showed O2+ PtF6-: PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2.

Bartlett looked up xenon's first ionisation energy and saw the near-equality with O2. He reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise Xe. The synthesis of yellow XePtF6 made the front page of Chemical & Engineering News.

Within months Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating Xe and F2 in a nickel container at 400°C. Today there are dozens of xenon compounds (XeO3, XeO4, XeF6, KrF2, ArF — the last only at cryogenic temperatures).

Helium and neon remain genuinely unreactive in normal conditions — their ionisation energies (2080 and 2370 kJ/mol) are too high for any known oxidiser to defeat.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.

items.title: Some enzymes work by tunnelling, not climbing
items.claim: Classical chemistry says reactions need energy to climb the activation barrier. But many enzymes — including alcohol dehydrogenase — transfer protons by quantum tunnelling THROUGH the barrier.
items.prompt: What's the smoking-gun evidence that proton tunnelling is happening in an enzyme?

options.text: The reaction happens even at absolute zero
Replacing the hydrogen with deuterium (twice the mass) slows the reaction far more than classical theory predicts — the kinetic isotope effect is anomalously huge
The enzyme glows when illuminated with UV light
The reaction speeds up when you cool it

items.reveal:
A particle's de Broglie wavelength scales as 1 over the square root of its mass. Deuterium is twice as heavy as protium, so its wavefunction decays into the barrier twice as quickly and its tunnelling probability collapses.

A classical activation-energy treatment predicts a deuterium-to-protium rate ratio of at most about 7 at room temperature. Several enzymes show ratios over 50 — only quantum tunnelling can explain this.

Quantum mechanics is doing serious work inside warm, wet, messy biological systems.
items.why: Students think quantum effects are confined to cold, isolated atoms in labs. In fact, they shape biochemistry at body temperature.

items.title: Frost forms by water vapour skipping the liquid state entirely
items.claim: Water vapour in cold air can deposit directly onto a windowpane as ice crystals without ever becoming liquid. The reverse — solid to gas without melting — is called sublimation, and is how freeze-drying works.
items.prompt: Why does water sometimes skip the liquid stage?

options.text: Water bends the laws of phase transitions
At pressures below the triple point (6.1 mbar for water) the liquid phase is not stable — water can only exist as solid or vapour, and transitions go directly between them
Frost forms only from existing ice
Liquid water is too dense for cold air

items.reveal_title: Below the triple point, liquid disappears
items.reveal:
Water's triple point sits at 0.01°C and 6.1 millibar — the only temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist. Below this pressure the liquid phase is unstable; water can only be vapour or ice, and crossing the boundary means sublimation or deposition.

At atmospheric pressure (1013 mbar) water can be liquid between 0 and 100°C, but small pockets of supercooled vapour near a cold surface can deposit straight to solid because the local equilibrium prefers ice over the metastable liquid intermediate.

Freeze-drying exploits this: freeze food, lower the pressure below the triple point, and the ice sublimes away with no melting. The structure is preserved, water is removed, and the result is light, stable food (instant coffee, astronaut meals, pharmaceutical formulations).
items.why: Solid to gas skipping liquid is treated as a curiosity. It is the dominant transition at low pressure and underpins multibillion-dollar industries.
